html:
A collection of about 200 laws of the Hittite kingdom in Anatolia, first written down about 1650 to 1500 BCE. The tablets were found at the Hittite capital Hattusa, in copies made over several centuries.

The laws cover murder, assault, theft, marriage, land, farm animals, wages and prices. Their striking feature is how often they set a payment instead of a bodily punishment. Many laws say what the penalty "formerly" was and what it is "now", usually a lower fine in silver or animals. The death penalty was kept for a few crimes, such as certain sexual offences and defying the king's court. Penalties differed for free people and slaves.

Compared with the Code of Hammurabi and its "eye for an eye", the Hittite laws look practical, more about making good the loss than about revenge. Like the earlier Code of Ur-Nammu, they were written in cuneiform, here in the Hittite language, the oldest written Indo-European language.
